title: Split Editor & Working With Multiple Files

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to view two or more files side by side in VS Code. This is how you'll follow along with course instructions while writing your own code — and how professional developers reference one file while editing another.

## Why Split the Editor?

Most of the time you'll be focused on one file. But situations where two files at once are essential include:

- **Following instructions while writing code.** Have the lesson notes on the left, your exercise file on the right.
- **HTML + CSS side by side.** Edit your HTML structure while keeping the CSS file visible.
- **Comparing two versions.** Before and after, or two different approaches.
- **JSON config + documentation.** The config file on one side, a reference doc on the other.
- **Diff view.** Seeing exactly what changed in a file before vs after a Git commit.

VS Code supports splitting the editor horizontally (top/bottom) or vertically (left/right). You can have as many splits as your screen allows — though two is the most practical for most tasks.

## How to Split the Editor

**Method 1 — Right-click a tab:**
1. Click on any open file tab at the top of the Editor Area
2. Right-click the tab
3. Select **Split Right** — the file opens in a new column to the right
4. In the right column's Explorer, click a different file to open it there

**Method 2 — Drag a tab:**
1. Click and hold on a file tab
2. Drag it to the right side of the editor — a blue indicator shows where it will land
3. Release — the file splits into a new column

**Method 3 — Keyboard shortcut:**
- Press **Ctrl+\** (backslash) to split the current file into a new column

**Method 4 — Menu:**
- View → Editor Layout → Two Columns

All four methods create a split view.

## Navigating Between Split Columns

Once you have two columns open:

- **Click** anywhere in a column to focus it — you can then type, scroll, and edit in that column
- **Ctrl+1** — focus the leftmost column
- **Ctrl+2** — focus the second column
- **Ctrl+3** — focus the third column (if you have three)

Each column has its own tabs. You can open multiple files in each column — they get their own tab row.

To close a split: click the X on every tab in that column, or drag all tabs back to the other column.

## Editor Layout Options

VS Code gives you full control over the layout:

- **Two Columns** (most common) — two side-by-side editors
- **Three Columns** — three side-by-side editors
- **Two Rows** — top/bottom split instead of left/right
- **Grid (2x2)** — four panels in a grid
- **Single** — back to one editor

To access these: View → Editor Layout → choose a layout.

For this course, Two Columns is all you need.

## Diff View: Seeing What Changed

VS Code has a built-in diff viewer — it shows you exactly what changed between two states of a file in a colour-coded side-by-side format.

**How to use it:**
1. In the Explorer panel, right-click a modified file
2. Click **Compare with Saved** — shows current unsaved changes vs the saved version

Or after a Git commit is set up (lesson 5-12):
1. Click the Source Control icon in the Activity Bar
2. Click any file listed under "Changes"
3. The diff view opens automatically, showing additions in green and removals in red

You'll use diff view constantly once you start using Git — it's how you review your own changes before committing them.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Coding
sections.content:
Set up a split editor and practise working in two files at once. **Step 1 — Open two files side by side:** 1. Make sure your `ai-course-projects` folder is open in VS Code 2. Click `hello.html` in the Explorer to open it 3. Right-click the `hello.html` tab at the top of the Editor Area 4. Click **Split Right** 5. Now click `README.md` in the Explorer — it opens in the right column 6. You should see `hello.html` on the left and `README.md` on the right **Step 2 — Edit both files:** 1. Click anywhere in the left column (hello.html) — the tab highlights to show it's focused 2. Press Ctrl+1 to confirm focus on the left 3. Make a small edit — change `

Hello, world!

` to `

Hello from VS Code!

` 4. Press Ctrl+S to save 5. Press Ctrl+2 to focus the right column 6. Add a line to README.md: `VS Code split editor works.` 7. Press Ctrl+S **Step 3 — Explore layouts:** 1. Click View in the menu bar → **Editor Layout** 2. Select **Two Rows** — the files are now top/bottom instead of left/right 3. Select **Two Columns** again to go back to side-by-side 4. Select **Single** to collapse back to one editor **Step 4 — Split with keyboard shortcut:** 1. Make sure only one editor column is open 2. Open `part-05-notes.md` 3. Press **Ctrl+\** (backslash) — the file splits 4. Click `prompt-experiments.md` in the Explorer to open it in the new column 5. Press Ctrl+1 and Ctrl+2 to confirm focus switching works **Check:** - [ ] Two files were open side by side - [ ] Ctrl+1 and Ctrl+2 switched focus between columns - [ ] You tried at least two layout options - [ ] Ctrl+\ split the editor

**Course workflow tip:** For the rest of this course, keep the lesson you're following in the left column and your exercise file in the right column. This lets you read and work simultaneously without switching windows. Many learners find this significantly speeds up their progress.

sections.title: Workshop A — Split Editor and File Comparison Drill
sections.content:
This 8-minute drill builds fluency with VS Code's multi-file view.

**Step 1 — Open two related files** (or create two text files with different content).

**Step 2 — Split the editor:** Ctrl+\ (backslash) splits the current file to the right. Now you see the same file in two panes.

**Step 3 — Move a file to the other pane:** Drag a tab from one pane to the other.

**Step 4 — Compare two files:** Ctrl+Shift+P → "Compare Active File with..." → select the second file. VS Code shows a diff view with changes highlighted.

**Step 5 — Work in both panes:** Write code in one pane while referencing another file in the other. This is the real workflow: reference documentation on the left, write code on the right.

**Step 6 — Ask Claude:** *"I often need to look at documentation or example code while writing my own. What VS Code layout and workflow would you recommend for this pattern?"*

sections.title: Workshop B — Reference-While-Building Workflow
sections.content:
Build a real piece of code while referencing an example or documentation in a split view — the most common advanced VS Code workflow.

**Step 1 — Identify a real task:** Something you're building where you'll reference example code, a tutorial, or a documentation file.

**Step 2 — Set up your split view:**
- Left pane: open the reference file (example code, docs, notes)
- Right pane: open a new file where you'll write your code

**Step 3 — Ask Claude to help you start:**
```
I want to build [describe what you're building]. I have these examples/docs as reference: [describe what's in your left pane]. 

Give me a skeleton structure for my implementation that I can fill in, looking at the reference as I go.
```

**Step 4 — Work with the split view:** Reference the left pane to understand patterns, write your implementation in the right pane.

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Once your implementation is complete, ask Claude: *"Compare my implementation to the reference code. Find 3 differences where I diverged from the pattern — are these intentional improvements or mistakes?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — Tab Groups and Layouts
sections.content:
VS Code supports complex multi-pane layouts that match your workflow.

**Step 1 — Create a 3-pane layout:**
- Main file: your code (centre)
- Left: file explorer
- Bottom: integrated terminal

**Step 2 — Move the panel to the right:** Ctrl+Shift+P → "View: Move Panel Right". Now terminal is on the right instead of bottom.

**Step 3 — Create Tab Groups:** Right-click a tab → "New Tab Group to the Right". You can have independent tab groups with different files open.

**Step 4 — Use Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2** to switch focus between editor panes without the mouse.

**Step 5 — Try the Zen Mode:** Ctrl+Shift+P → "View: Toggle Zen Mode". Full screen, no distractions. Useful for reading and understanding complex code.

**Step 6 — Find your preferred layout** for your most common task and write it down. Recreate it at the start of each work session.

sections.title: Workshop D — Build a VS Code Workflow for AI Code Review
sections.content:
Set up a specific VS Code layout optimised for reviewing AI-generated code.

**Step 1 — The AI code review layout:**
- Left pane: the AI-generated code file
- Right pane: a review notes file (create review.md)
- Bottom: terminal for running/testing the code

**Step 2 — Create review.md** as a template:
```markdown
# Code Review Notes

## Correctness Issues
- [ ] 

## Security Concerns  
- [ ] 

## Performance Problems
- [ ] 

## Missing Error Handling
- [ ] 

## Questions for AI
- [ ] 
```

**Step 3 — Read the AI-generated code** line by line in the left pane. Write notes in the right pane.

**Step 4 — Run the code** in the bottom terminal and note any runtime errors.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude to review it too:** Paste the code and your notes and ask: *"Here is AI-generated code [paste] and my initial review notes [paste]. What did I miss? What are the 3 most important issues I should address first?"*

sections.question: You have 15 files open as tabs in VS Code and it's getting hard to navigate. What are two good strategies?
options: Close VS Code and reopen with fewer files
Use Ctrl+P to jump to files by name, and organise related files into tab groups
Open a new VS Code window for each group of files
Switch to a simpler editor with fewer features
sections.explanation: Two effective strategies: Ctrl+P (Go to File) lets you jump to any file by typing its name — faster than scanning many tabs. Tab groups let you organise related files (e.g., frontend files in one group, backend files in another) so each group shows a manageable number of tabs. VS Code also has "pinned tabs" to keep frequently used files accessible and "preview mode" (single-click opens a temporary preview tab).

sections.question: You want to compare yesterday's version of a file to today's to see what changed. What VS Code feature does this?
options: File → History (not a real VS Code feature)
Use git: `git diff` in the terminal or VS Code's Source Control panel to see changes between commits
The VS Code Timeline (View → Open View → Timeline) shows file history and git diff for each entry
sections.explanation: VS Code's Timeline view shows the history of a file, including git commits. Click any commit to see a diff of what changed. The Source Control panel (Ctrl+Shift+G) also shows all changed files with inline diffs. For comparing two specific commits, use `git diff commit1 commit2 filename` in the terminal or the GitLens extension for a richer GUI experience.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 5-11.** You can now split your editor and work on two files at once. This is your last lesson before the most important one in this part: VS Code's Git integration.
